posts.description:
Your QA tests aren’t flaky because of “bad tests.”

They’re flaky because of bad data.

Most teams don’t realize how much their QA environment is working against them — long run times, inconsistent results, random failures… all of it usually comes back to one thing:

👉  The way you seed your test data.

After reviewing hundreds of customer setups at Rainforest, one pattern became impossible to ignore:

🐄 Teams that treat their test data like cattle scale.
🐕 Teams that treat it like pets don’t.

We broke down the most common mistakes (and the fixes) in this carousel.

Tell us: Do you find this to be true in your QA environment?

P.S. If you want the full deep dive, check out Keith Johnson's post on our blog.

posts.name: Here’s how functional testing keeps your app from falling apart, one mock at a time. | Uma Abu
posts.description: Here’s how functional testing keeps your app from falling apart, one mock at a time.
posts.transcript: Software testing generally falls under 2 broad categories, functional and nonfunctional testing. Let's start with the first functional testing. Functional testing checks that the software behaves the way it's supposed to. It's about making sure inputs produce the right outputs and that feature is work according to their requirement. Let's say we're building a file sharing approval app for team. Users should be able to log in, upload documents, trigger an approval workflow, and eventually archive the file. Functional testing would verify that users can log in with the valid credentials. Upload files, review them, kick off approvals, and archive the document. When they're done, each step is validated to make sure it does what it's supposed to do. Now let's look at some type of functional testing. The 1st is unit test. Unit test at the foundation. They focus on the smallest piece of code, individual functions, methods, or modules, and verify that they work in isolation. For example, you might have a function like this that checks whether a document upload is valid. The function checks the file name, file extension, and the file size. Unit test for the function might look. Something like this where we check various combinations of the file name and sizes to confirm the logic is correct and working how we expect it to. Unit tests are written by developers during development. They allow bugs to be caught early and make it easier to debug issues since failure the scope to just a specific piece of code. But not everything should be unit tested. A common mistake is writing unit tests that incorporate external systems like API calls, databases, or file storage. This is an anti pattern because those systems can introduce flaky tests tests that can sometimes. Or sometimes fail, often due to things outside your control like networking stability or service downtime. To avoid this, we use mocking. Mock simulate the behavior of external systems so you can focus on the logic in your code instead of connecting to a real database. To test login logic, you can mark a database call to return a valid user or an error and test how your code responds. Now once the individual units work, the next step is to make sure they work together. And that's where integration testing comes in. It checks that components interact correctly for our file sharing. Up. We might write integration tests to verify that after uploading a file, the system kicks off an approval workflow and logs the event in the activity log O I'm. Integration tests can also include interactions with external systems, like calling third party APIs and making sure the response is processed correctly. It's all about making sure the seams between the parts of your systems work correctly.

posts.description:
🚀 QA/Automation Engineer
Flaky Playwright tests are not just a testing problem — they are a confidence problem.
In real-world automation, a test that passes 9/10 times can be more dangerous than an obvious failure because it creates noise, wasted debugging time, and unreliable CI/CD feedback.

Here are the techniques I use to make Playwright automation more stable:
🔹 1. Use Playwright auto-waiting instead of unnecessary hard waits
🔹 2. Use resilient locators like getByRole(), getByLabel() and getByTestId()
🔹 3. Handle dynamic content with condition-based waits
🔹 4. Control external dependencies using API mocking/routing
🔹 5. Keep tests isolated with independent test data and fixtures
🔹 6. Use retries wisely — retries should diagnose noise, not hide defects
🔹 7. Write user-focused assertions instead of implementation-dependent assertions
🔹 8. Capture traces, screenshots, videos and logs for faster RCA
🔹 9. Stabilize the test environment — browser, data, network and services
🔹 10. Use Claude as an AI pair for automation — refactoring flaky tests, analysing failures, improving locators and suggesting better waits/assertions.

🤖 Example Claude prompt
“Analyze this failed Playwright test, trace, error log and screenshot. Identify the likely root cause of flakiness, explain why it happens intermittently, and refactor the test using Playwright best practices. Do not simply add a timeout.”

The goal isn't simply to make tests green.
The goal is to build automation that is:
✅ Reliable
✅ Maintainable
✅ Debug
✅ Fast
✅ CI/CD friendly
✅ Trustworthy

Good automation doesn't just pass tests — it builds confidence in every release.
🎯 What recruiters can see from this
This approach demonstrates practical experience with:
Playwright + TypeScript/JavaScript + CI/CD + Test Design + Debugging + API Mocking + Test Stability + AI-assisted Automation

I'm continuously exploring how AI + modern automation practices can improve software quality and reduce repetitive QA effort.
What is the most common cause of flaky tests in your automation framework? 👇

#Playwright #QAEngineer #TestAutomation #AutomationTesting #QualityEngineering #SoftwareTesting #TypeScript #JavaScript #ClaudeAI #AIinTesting #AITesting #SDET #QualityAssurance #CICD #TestAutomationEngineer

A flaky test does not only waste time.

It teaches the team to ignore failures.

The first time a test fails unexpectedly, someone investigates.

The fifth time, someone simply clicks “rerun.”

And when it passes, everyone moves on.

That is where the real risk begins.

A flaky test slowly changes the team’s behaviour:

• red pipelines stop feeling urgent
• reruns replace investigation
• release decisions become less reliable
• real product bugs can be dismissed as “probably flaky”

First rerun: investigation.
Fifth rerun: team ritual.

In my experience, flaky tests need the same things as product bugs:

• a clear owner
• a documented reason for failure
• a deadline for fixing or removing them
• separation between test instability and actual product behaviour

Temporarily isolating a test may be necessary.

Leaving it forgotten is not.

The most important automation metric is not how many tests passed.

It is whether the team still trusts a failure when one appears.

How does your team handle flaky tests: fix, quarantine, or keep rerunning until they turn green?

posts.description:
“End-to-end testing is one of the more common approaches to testing software, but it is complex, fragile expensive and low quality. As soon as we accept that the best way to test our system is to deploy it all together, with everything else that it interacts with and then try broad-brush interactions with the whole lot, we have lost control. To do a great job of testing we need much finer-grained control, and so need to reject E2E testing. Great automated testing depends on us controlling the variables, and ATDD, TDD and BDD rely on our ability to synthesize inputs and collect outputs from our system so that we can test it. E2E testing stops us from doing that.”

comments.author: li-user-31
comments.text:
From an OM point of view, something I try to stress to organizations: Whatever your bottleneck is, you can divide your entire annual revenue into the unit flow rate of your bottleneck. That's how valuable it is. 

Every defect that is discovered *after* the final stage of production, whether by a customer or a "PROD QA tester", represents one unit that you have to pay *TWICE* to pass through the bottleneck. 

AND, time lost at the bottleneck can never be recovered. Each defect pushes the entire queue of all future work "back by one unit". This count accumulates permanently for as long as you're in business. You can never get that queue time back. Ever. 

The only solution is to move QA so far "to the left" that you put it *before* the production process. Which is to say — TDD.

From Chaos to Clarity: How Testopedia Tackles Flaky Tests Across Monorepos

A few years ago, we embarked on a journey to eliminate flaky code tests at Uber, with the goals of stabilizing continuous integration across mono-repos, raising the quality bar, and resolving  Bermuda Triangles of unclear test accountabilities. Flaky tests are insidious. At best, they cause developers to toil over logs for each release, and at worst, obscure meaningful signals with excessive noise.

Testopedia, a tool built at Uber, has helped us to fix such issues, as described in the Uber blog. Testopedia analyzes testing logs and statistics, dashboards insights, and alerts teams of regressions and problems.
